raw_record.question_text: The diagram shows part of a river which has two islands in it. There are six bridges linking the islands and the two banks as shown. Leonhard goes for a walk every day in which he walks over each bridge exactly once. He always starts at point A, goes first over bridge 1 and always finishes at point B. What is the maximum number of days that he can walk without repeating the order in which he crosses the bridges?

method.method_draft: Convert the diagram into a multigraph. From the image, identify four land vertices: top bank, bottom bank, left island, and right island. Bridges are edges: 1 connects top bank to left island, 2 connects left island to bottom bank, 3 and 4 both connect the two islands, 5 connects right island to top bank, and 6 connects right island to bottom bank. From the text, Leonhard must start at A, cross bridge 1 first, use every bridge exactly once, and finish at B, so the last bridge must be 5. After bridge 1 he is on the left island, and before bridge 5 he must be on the right island. Thus count Euler trails in the remaining subgraph using bridges 2, 3, 4, 6 from left island to right island. Case on the first remaining bridge: if it is 2, then 6 must follow, then 3 and 4 can be crossed in either order, giving 2 orders. If it is 3, then either 4 then 2 then 6, or 6 then 2 then 4, giving 2 orders. If it is 4, symmetrically gives 2 orders. Total 2 + 2 + 2 = 6 possible bridge orders, so the maximum number of days is 6.

method.method_draft: Use a block-counting argument on the middle four bridges. From the image, after crossing bridge 1 from A, Leonhard is on the left island, and to finish at B by bridge 5 he must be on the right island just before the last crossing. The middle bridges are 2, 3, 4, and 6. Bridges 2 and 6 are the only remaining bridges touching the lower bank, so whenever the walk goes to the lower bank by one of them, it must immediately leave by the other; therefore bridges 2 and 6 must occur consecutively as one forced block. This block acts like a move between the two islands: from the left island it must be 2 then 6, while from the right island it must be 6 then 2. Bridges 3 and 4 are also individual moves between the two islands. So the middle of the walk consists of three island-switching moves: bridge 3, bridge 4, and the {2,6} block. These three moves can be arranged in any of 3! = 6 orders; in each arrangement the orientation of the {2,6} block is forced by the island Leonhard is on. Thus there are 6 valid complete bridge orders.
